1.title: Design the Data Model
1.text: Welcome to Module five: Design the Data Model. It covers the exam area Model the data. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Configure table and column properties. Implement role-playing dimensions. Define a relationship's cardinality and cross-filter direction. Create a common date table. Identify use cases for calculated columns and calculated tables. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Model the data (twenty-five-thirty percent). Exam format: a one hundred-minute proctored exam; a score of seven hundred on a scale to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official P L three hundred study guide, skills measured as of April twenty, twenty twenty-six.

1.title: Table and column properties
1.text: Table and column properties. The data model is the set of tables, relationships and calculations behind your reports. Good design starts with the properties of each table and column, which you set in Model view, in the Properties pane or on the Column tools tab.

1.title: Table and column properties, continued
1.text: Table and column properties. The figure shows this: A star schema with one Sales fact table, dimension tables on the one side, and a Date table used in two roles.

1.title: Table and column properties, continued
1.text: Table and column properties. Data category. What it does: Tells visuals how to treat the values. Example: City lets a map place it; Web U R L makes a link. Sort by column. What it does: Orders one column by another column of the same table. Example: Month Name sorted by Month Number. Default summarization. What it does: How a field is aggregated when you drag it into a visual. Example: Sum, Average, Minimum, Maximum, Count, Count (Distinct) or Do not summarize.

1.title: Table and column properties, continued
1.text: Table and column properties. Format. What it does: Display format, decimals and symbols. Example: Currency, percentage, date. Hide. What it does: Removes the field from the Report view field list. Example: Hide keys and helper columns. Display folder. What it does: Groups fields into folders in the Fields pane. Example: A folder named Sales Metrics. Description. What it does: Text shown as a tooltip when you hover over the field. Example: Explains what a measure means.

1.title: Table and column properties, continued
1.text: Table and column properties. Is key. What it does: Marks the column that uniquely identifies each row. Example: Product Key in the Product table. Hierarchy. What it does: An ordered set of columns for drill down. Example: Category, Subcategory, Product.

1.title: Table and column properties, continued
1.text: Table and column properties. Numeric columns default to Sum. That is wrong for keys and for a year column, so set them to Do not summarize (the menu label reads Don't summarize). A hierarchy needs all its columns in the same table, because hierarchies cannot span tables. Exam tip: Sort by column fixes a text column that sorts alphabetically, such as month names ordered by month number. Set keys and years to Do not summarize so they are not added up. Exam tip: A hidden field is hidden only from the Report view field list. It still works in relationships and dacks, and a user with Build permission on the semantic model can still see it.

1.title: Role-playing dimensions
1.text: Role-playing dimensions. A role-playing dimension is one dimension used in more than one role. A Sales table with Order Date and Ship Date relates to one Date table twice. Power B I allows only one active relationship between two tables. The active one is a solid line; the others are inactive and drawn dashed.

1.title: Role-playing dimensions, continued
1.text: Role-playing dimensions. use relationship. How it works: Keep one Date table; a measure turns on the inactive relationship inside calculate. Trade-off: Smaller model, but you need one measure per role, and a Date slicer filters only the active role.

1.title: Role-playing dimensions, continued
1.text: Role-playing dimensions. One dimension table per role (recommended). How it works: Create an Order Date and a Ship Date table, as referenced queries or calculated tables, and rename columns to be self-describing. Trade-off: Every role has its own slicers and relationship; the model is slightly larger.

1.title: Role-playing dimensions, continued
1.text: Role-playing dimensions. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: Only one relationship between two tables can be active. An inactive one is used only inside a measure through use relationship. Microsoft recommends one dimension table per role.

1.title: Cardinality and cross-filter direction
1.text: Cardinality and cross-filter direction. Cardinality describes how many rows match on each side of a relationship. One-to-many. Meaning: One dimension row matches many fact rows. Note: Default in a star schema; fastest. Many-to-one. Meaning: The same relationship seen from the fact table. Note: Behaves the same. One-to-one. Meaning: Each row matches at most one row on the other side. Note: Always filters both ways; consider merging the tables. Many-to-many. Meaning: Neither column holds unique values. Note: Slowest; use a bridge table when you can.

1.title: Cardinality and cross-filter direction, continued
1.text: Cardinality and cross-filter direction. The column on the one side must be unique. Duplicate values there make the refresh fail, so add an index (surrogate key) column in Power Query if needed. Key columns on both sides need the same data type, and date keys should not carry a time part. Cross-filter direction controls how filters travel.

1.title: Cardinality and cross-filter direction, continued
1.text: Cardinality and cross-filter direction. Single. Filters flow from the one side to the many side (default and recommended). Both. Filters flow in both directions; a one-to-one relationship is always Both. Both is risky. It can create ambiguous filter paths, slow the queries and give surprising totals. Prefer Single, and use the cross filter function inside one measure when you need Both only there. The setting Apply security filter in both directions exists only for row-level security. Assume referential integrity (Direct Query, no N U L Ls on the many side) allows an inner join. Exam tip: Filters flow from the one side to the many side. Duplicates in the one-side column stop the refresh; a many-to-many relationship is the slowest; use Both only when a scenario truly needs it.

1.title: Create a common date table
1.text: Create a common date table. A common date table is one Date dimension that every fact table relates to. It is the foundation of time intelligence. Dates. Unique and contiguous: one row per day, no gaps, no duplicates. Nulls. None. Data type. Date or Date or Time, covering all the dates in your data. Mark as date table. Table tools, then Mark as date table, then pick the Date column. Relationship. One-to-many from the Date column to the fact table's date column, same type, no time part.

1.title: Create a common date table, continued
1.text: Create a common date table. calendar builds a table from a start date and an end date you give. calendar auto finds the range from the date columns in the model; an optional argument sets the last month of the fiscal year, so calendar auto(six) fits a June year end. You can also build the table in Power Query or load it from the source.

1.title: Create a common date table, continued
1.text: Create a common date table. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

2.title: Create a common date table, continued
2.text: Create a common date table. Auto date or time creates a hidden date table for every date column. This makes the model bigger, so turn it off in the Data Load options once you have a real date table. Marking your table as the date table removes the hidden one. A Direct Query model has no automatic date hierarchy, so it needs a date table. Exam tip: calendar needs a start and an end date; calendar auto detects the range and takes an optional fiscal year end month. Mark the table as the date table, and turn auto date or time off to keep the model small.

2.title: Calculated columns and calculated tables
2.text: Calculated columns and calculated tables. Calculated column. When it is computed: Per row, at refresh; stored in the model and uses memory. Best use: A value you filter, group, slice or relate by. Measure. When it is computed: At query time, in the filter context; nothing stored. Best use: Totals, ratios and other aggregations. Calculated table. When it is computed: A dacks table expression stored in the model; recalculated when its source tables refresh. Best use: Date table, role-playing copy, bridge or helper table.

2.title: Calculated columns and calculated tables, continued
2.text: Calculated columns and calculated tables. Power Query custom column. When it is computed: During refresh, as part of loading. Best use: Preferred when possible.

2.title: Calculated columns and calculated tables, continued
2.text: Calculated columns and calculated tables. Power Query is preferred when possible. Its columns compress better and are part of the refresh. Use dacks when you need a measure or a dacks only function, such as related, or logic that depends on other tables in the model. A calculated column can be used in a slicer, an axis, a filter or a relationship; a measure cannot. Exam tip: A calculated column is stored and computed per row; a measure is computed at query time. If a value goes on an axis or slicer it must be a column; if it is a total that reacts to filters it must be a measure.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A matrix shows month names in alphabetical order, so April comes before January. The Date table also has a Month Number column. What should you do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Set Month Name to sort by the Month Number column. The Sort by column property orders a text column by a numeric column of the same table, and the other options do not change the sort order.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A Sales table has Order Date and Ship Date, and both relate to one Date table with Order Date as the active relationship. A measure must total sales by ship date. What should you use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: calculate with use relationship on the Ship Date column. use relationship turns on the inactive relationship for the duration of that calculation.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. An author sets every relationship in a star schema to Both so that all filters reach all tables. What is the most likely result? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Ambiguous filter paths and slower queries in large models. Bi-directional filtering can create ambiguity and hurt performance, so Single is the better default.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A finance team's fiscal year ends in June. You need a Date table that covers every date in the model. Which expression should you use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: calendar auto with six as the fiscal year end month. calendar auto finds the date range itself and accepts the last month of the fiscal year.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A Customer table gets its data from a sequel view. A dacks calculated column that joins First Name and Last Name inflates the model. What should you do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Build the same logic as a Power Query column. Power Query columns compress better than dacks calculated columns and are built in at refresh, so they are preferred when possible.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Report users want to drill from Category to Subcategory to Product in one visual. All three columns are in the Product table. What should you create? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: A hierarchy that holds the three columns. A hierarchy orders columns of one table for drill down, whereas a display folder only groups fields in the Fields pane.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Which property sorts Month Name by Month Number? Answer: Sort by column. Question two. How many active relationships can exist between two tables? Answer: One. Question three. Which function turns on an inactive relationship inside a measure? Answer: use relationship.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What are the two cross-filter directions? Answer: Single and Both. Question five. Which dacks function builds a date table from the dates already in the model? Answer: calendar auto. Question six. When is a calculated column computed, and where is it kept? Answer: At refresh, and it is stored in the model.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Column properties: Data category, Sort by column, Default summarization (Do not summarize for keys), Format, Hide, Display folder, Description, Is key. Hierarchy: Columns of one table only; used for drill down. Role-playing: One active relationship only; use relationship for the others; one table per role is recommended. Cardinality: One-to-many is the default and fastest; the one side must be unique. Direction: Single by default (one side to many side); Both can be ambiguous and slow. Date table: Unique, contiguous dates, no nulls, marked as date table; calendar or calendar auto. Calculated column: Per row, stored, usable on axes, slicers and relationships. Measure and table: Measure at query time; calculated table stored; Power Query preferred.
